---
title: Counterbalancing
subtitle: Modeling random assignment, block ordering, and counterbalanced designs
---

Random assignment is a control-flow operation: the participant goes down one path rather than another, by chance. In Studyflow, this maps to the `RandomGateway` element. This guide covers the three patterns you will use most often.

## Random assignment to groups

The simplest case: every participant is randomly assigned to one of two (or more) conditions.

Drop a `cognitive:RandomGateway` after the demographics block. Add an outgoing sequence flow for each condition. The inspector lets you set the probability on each branch (default: equal). The browser runner draws a branch at execution time and routes the participant down exactly one of them. The draw is seeded by the study's `studyflow:seed`, so a pinned seed makes the allocation replayable (a `?seed=` in the run link overrides it).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Diagram (TODO)"}
A simple two-group random assignment diagram should live at `docs/assets/img/guides/random-assignment.svg`. The element catalog already has [`random_gateway_pattern.svg`](../assets/img/elements/random_gateway_pattern.svg) which illustrates the basic shape.
:::

For balanced (not just random) assignment, set the gateway's `algorithm` to `round-robin` instead of the default `probabilistic`: allocation cycles through the branches rather than drawing independently per participant.

## Block-level counterbalancing

When you have several task blocks (say A, B, C) and want every participant to do all of them, but in a randomized order, enumerate the orderings you care about (ABC, ACB, BAC, …) as separate sub-flows downstream of a `cognitive:RandomGateway`. Each branch contains the blocks in one specific order, and the branch is drawn from the study's `studyflow:seed` like any other random assignment. This is explicit, reviewable, and it runs -- the diagram is the spec.

It is also verbose: *k* blocks means up to *k*! branches. For more blocks than you care to draw, enumerate only the orderings the design actually needs (e.g. a Latin square over 4 blocks is 4 branches, not 24), or move the ordering inside a single task's `configurations` -- see [Counterbalancing across trials](#counterbalancing-across-trials) below.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
## Parallel gateways do not execute today

A `bpmn:ParallelGateway` is drawable and exports fine, but the browser runner raises an error on it during traversal, so a parallel-fork-and-permute pattern is design-only for now. Keep randomized ordering on a `RandomGateway`.
:::

## Stratified randomization

Stratification means: keep the random assignment balanced *within* subgroups. For example, balance gender within each treatment arm.

Stratification is a parameter on the random gateway, not a gateway type of its own: set `stratifyBy` on a `cognitive:RandomGateway` to the variable that partitions the cohort (`age_band`, `sex`, ...) and list the strata in `strata`. The *Stratified allocation* palette template is a `RandomGateway` with those fields prefilled. Note that the browser runner currently treats such a gateway as a plain random pick -- the stratification is declared in the diagram but not yet enforced at run time.

The alternative, which the browser runner does execute, is to draw it: branch first on the stratification variable (an `Exclusive` gateway on `sex`, say), then run an independent `RandomGateway` inside each branch. The diagram then makes it visually obvious that randomization is happening per-stratum.

## Counterbalancing across trials

For trial-level counterbalancing within a single task (e.g., congruent vs incongruent Stroop trials in random order), keep the counterbalancing *inside the task* rather than expressing it in the diagram. Studyflow diagrams describe study-level structure; trial-level randomization is a parameter on the `CognitiveTask` activity. See the [Cognitive tasks example](../examples/cognitive-tasks.qmd) for trial-level structure.

## Checklist

- [ ] Every random gateway has at least two outgoing flows.
- [ ] Probabilities on the outgoing flows sum to 1.
- [ ] If using stratification, the stratifying gateway is upstream of the random gateway.
- [ ] `algorithm` is `round-robin` if you want balanced (not independent) assignment.
- [ ] The downstream end events handle every branch (no dead-end paths).
